summary: AstroView is offline software that helps astronauts monitor and prepare for Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), the eye changes seen in many long-duration crew members. In-flight eye exams are weeks apart, so gradual vision change can go unnoticed. AstroView fills that gap with short daily vision checks scored against each astronaut's own baseline, green/yellow/red alerts with the reasons behind them, and a one-page summary for the flight surgeon. Its core is training: adaptive drills and a 3-minute, 180-day Mission Run blur near vision along the hyperopic shift reported in SANS (+0.50 to +1.75 D), so crews practise reading instruments, medicine labels and alarms, and practise the right response, before it happens. Eye-emergency drills based on real spacewalk incidents add step-by-step response training. This matters most on Moon and Mars missions, where communication delays of up to about 22 minutes mean crews must monitor and respond on their own. AstroView does not diagnose, prevent or treat SANS; all demo data is simulated.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AstroView is an offline web app that helps astronauts monitor and prepare for Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). It combines four things in one place:

1. Daily check (3-5 min): near vision, contrast sensitivity, near-far focus switching and an Amsler grid, plus a symptom log. Each result is scored against the astronaut's own baseline (mean of the first 3 days).

2. Early warning: yellow when the 7-day average is below 90% of baseline for 3 days or symptoms appear on 3 of the last 7 days; red when it is below 80% for 3 days with symptoms. Every alert shows the numbers behind it. These are starter thresholds, to be tuned with clinicians.

3. Flight surgeon summary: one page with status, reasons, a 30-day trend and countermeasure adherence, exportable as PDF, with no raw data.

4. Training, organised as a 5-stage curriculum: understand SANS (vision simulator, micro-lessons), daily baseline check, 8 adaptive vision drills under simulated blur, eye emergency protocol drills, and Mission Run.

HOW IT WORKS

Blur is computed from geometric optics: blur size = pupil diameter x dioptres of defocus at a 40 cm reading distance, converted to on-screen pixels. Drills use adaptive staircases to keep accuracy near 70-80%, as in sports and perceptual-learning training, and can train beyond the SANS range (up to +2.50 D). Safety rules enforce a 60-second break every 5 minutes, a 15-minute daily cap, and a stop button for eye strain, headache or nausea. The demo uses a synthetic 180-day mission that turns yellow on day 109 and red on day 134, before the day-150 eye exam.

CREATIVITY

- Mission Run: a 180-day mission in 3 minutes. Near vision blurs day by day along the hyperopic shift reported in SANS (+0.50 to +1.75 D) while the user completes 8 real crew tasks (gauges, medicine labels, valve codes, stacked alarms). The monitoring alerts fire on schedule, coping aids unlock (larger text, a +1.00 D reading lens, partner cross-check), and the user decides whether to notify the flight surgeon. A debrief shows a readiness score and the dioptre level where errors began.

- Eye emergency drills: four scenarios in which the user picks the right actions in order while the view through the helmet worsens, based on public accounts of real spacewalks (Chris Hadfield, STS-100, 2001; Luca Parmitano, 2013). Fatal options such as opening the visor or unclipping the tether are marked. These are training designs, not official NASA procedures.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

AstroView fills the data gap between scheduled in-flight eye exams, gives crews and flight surgeons an early signal with reasons, and builds task skills for working with blurred near vision. It runs fully offline on the tablets crews already use, which matters most on Moon and Mars missions, where one-way communication delays reach about 22 minutes and solar conjunction can cut contact for 2-3 weeks.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty: AstroView does not diagnose, prevent or treat SANS. Screen tests cannot detect optic disc swelling; that needs OCT and a clinician. The training benefit for SANS is a hypothesis to be tested. All demo data is simulated.

- Crew time: core use is 3-5 minutes a day; training is optional and capped.

- Privacy: data stays on the device; the surgeon summary contains summary data only.

- Validation plan: (1) bench test of on-screen size accuracy; (2) about 30 healthy volunteers wearing +0.50 to +1.50 D lenses to test detection, test-retest reliability and trained vs untrained performance; (3) ground analog such as head-down-tilt bed rest or NASA HERA, compared with OCT; (4) ISS technology demonstration reviewed by flight surgeons.

- Accessibility: Thai and English interface, large touch targets, status shown by text and shape as well as colour, reduced-motion support.

TOOLS

React web app (Progressive Web App with IndexedDB and a service worker), vanilla JavaScript modules for the training layer, SVG charts, HTML and CSS.
